lede: Exploding an array to work on each item gives you more rows than you started with. Higher-order functions work on every item of an array in place, so each row stays one row.
objectives: Change every item of an array with `F.transform`
Keep only some items of an array with `F.filter`
Ask whether any or every item passes a test with `F.exists` and `F.forall`
Fold an array into one value with `F.aggregate`, starting from the right type

blocks.md:
The shop's event tables keep lists inside a row. In `cart_events` and `checkout_events`, `items` is an array of structs, one per product, each with a `sku`, a `qty` and a `price`. In `searches`, `filters` is an array of text.

A **higher-order function** takes an array column and a Python function, written as a `lambda`, and applies the function to the items for you. Inside the lambda, `x` stands for one item, so `x["sku"]` is that item's `sku` field. The lambda doesn't run in Python: Spark turns it into a column expression and runs it on every row.

`F.transform(array, lambda x: ...)` gives a new array with one result per item, in the same order.

blocks.title: One value from each item
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

skus = cart_events.select("event_id", "action", F.transform("items", lambda x: x["sku"]).alias("skus"))
skus.show(truncate=False)
blocks.note: Each row still has one array; it just holds the `sku` of each item instead of the whole struct. CA-0003 had two items, so it has two skus.

blocks.md: The lambda can work out anything a column can: arithmetic, other functions, struct fields. Multiplying an item's `qty` by its `price` gives the value of that line of the basket.

blocks.title: Arithmetic on every item
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

lines = cart_events.select(
    "event_id",
    F.transform("items", lambda x: x["qty"] * x["price"]).alias("line_values"),
)
lines.show(truncate=False)
blocks.note: CA-0002 added two items at 11.99, so its line is worth 23.98. `qty` is a whole number and `price` a `double`, so the result is a `double`.

blocks.md:
`F.filter(array, lambda x: condition)` keeps the items where the condition is true, in their order. It's the array version of filtering rows: the row stays, only its array gets shorter. A condition is a comparison such as `x["qty"] > 1` or `f != "in_stock"`.

Functions chain: filter first, then transform what's left.

blocks.title: Keep some items
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

searches.select("event_id", "filters", F.filter("filters", lambda f: f != "in_stock").alias("other_filters")).show(truncate=False)

multi = F.filter("items", lambda x: x["qty"] > 1)
checkout_events.select("event_id", F.transform(multi, lambda x: x["sku"]).alias("multi_skus")).show()
blocks.note: SR-0002's only filter was `in_stock`, so nothing is left: an empty array, not a missing one. In each checkout of CO-0001 to CO-0003, only SKU-1013 was bought more than once.

blocks.md:
Sometimes you want one yes-or-no answer per row:

- `F.exists(array, lambda x: condition)` is true when **at least one** item passes.
- `F.forall(array, lambda x: condition)` is true when **every** item passes.

An empty array has no item that fails, so `forall` is true for it, and no item that passes, so `exists` is false.

blocks.title: Any item, every item
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

checkout_events.select(
    "event_id",
    F.exists("items", lambda x: x["qty"] > 1).alias("any_multiple"),
    F.forall("items", lambda x: x["price"] < 100).alias("all_under_100"),
).show()

searches.select(
    "event_id",
    "filters",
    F.exists("filters", lambda f: f == "in_stock").alias("has_in_stock"),
    F.forall("filters", lambda f: f != "in_stock").alias("no_in_stock"),
).show(truncate=False)
blocks.note: CO-0004's single item costs 119.95, so not every price is under 100. SR-0003 and SR-0005 have no filters: `exists` is false and `forall` is true.

blocks.md:
`F.aggregate(array, start, lambda acc, x: ...)` folds an array into one value. It starts with `start`, then for each item works out a new `acc` (short for accumulator) from the old one and the item. Adding up a field is the most common use.

The start value sets the type of the answer. `F.lit(0)` is a whole number, which is right for adding `qty`; to add `double` prices, start from `F.lit(0.0)`. The same functions exist in SQL text, with `x -> ...` for the lambda.

blocks.title: Fold the basket into totals
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

checkout_events.select(
    "event_id",
    F.aggregate("items", F.lit(0), lambda acc, x: acc + x["qty"]).alias("units"),
    F.aggregate("items", F.lit(0.0), lambda acc, x: acc + x["qty"] * x["price"]).alias("basket_value"),
).show()

checkout_events.selectExpr("event_id", "aggregate(items, 0, (acc, x) -> acc + x.qty) AS units").show()
blocks.note: CO-0001 has one item at 89.00 and two at 11.99: 3 units worth 112.98, the same as its `order_total`. The SQL line gives the same `units`.

blocks.title: A whole-number start for a double sum
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

checkout_events.select(F.aggregate("items", F.lit(0), lambda acc, x: acc + x["price"]).alias("total")).show()
blocks.note: `F.lit(0)` makes the accumulator a whole number, but adding a `double` price gives a `double`, and the accumulator can't change type halfway. Start from `F.lit(0.0)` instead.

blocks.md: One more thing to know with real data: a missing value inside the lambda behaves as it does anywhere else. If an item's `qty` is missing, `acc + x["qty"]` is missing, and so is the final total. If the whole array is missing, every one of these functions returns a missing value too.

concept.prompt: What does `F.transform("items", lambda x: x["sku"])` give for a row whose `items` holds three structs?
choices: One array of three skus, in the items' order
concept.why: `transform` keeps one row and returns an array with one result per item, in order. Exploding is what turns items into rows.

concept.prompt: A search has an empty `filters` array. What do `F.exists("filters", lambda f: f == "in_stock")` and `F.forall("filters", lambda f: f == "in_stock")` give?
concept.why: An empty array has no item that passes, so `exists` is false, and no item that fails, so `forall` is true.

concept.prompt: Why does `F.aggregate("items", F.lit(0), lambda acc, x: acc + x["price"])` fail when `price` is a `double`?
choices: The start value makes the accumulator a whole number, and adding a double changes its type
`price` can't be read inside a lambda
concept.why: The start value fixes the accumulator's type. `F.lit(0)` is a whole number; adding a `double` gives a `double`, so Spark refuses. Start from `F.lit(0.0)`.

review: Higher-order functions take an array column and a `lambda`, and work on each item without adding rows.
`F.transform(arr, lambda x: ...)` returns one result per item, in order. `x["field"]` reads a field of a struct item.
`F.filter(arr, lambda x: cond)` keeps the items where the condition is true. An array with nothing left is empty, not missing.
`F.exists` is true when at least one item passes; `F.forall` when every item does. On an empty array they give false and true.
`F.aggregate(arr, start, lambda acc, x: ...)` folds an array into one value. The start value sets the type: `F.lit(0)` for whole numbers, `F.lit(0.0)` for doubles.
A missing value inside the lambda makes the result missing, and a missing array gives a missing answer.
